title: Inheritance (single base class)
hook: When one type is truly a specialized version of another, you write `class Derived : Base`. C# gives you exactly one base class, and constructors must chain with `base(...)` before the derived type finishes initializing.

blocks.text: **Inheritance** lets a derived class reuse and extend a base class. The syntax is `class Derived : Base`. The derived type gets the base's accessible members — public, protected, and internal — but **not** constructors or finalizers. C# allows only **one** base class; you can also list multiple interfaces after the base class name.

entries.plainDefinition: The parent type that another class derives from. Also called superclass or parent class.
entries.example: `class LtiHandler : AuthHandler` — AuthHandler is the base class.

entries.plainDefinition: A class that inherits from a base class. Also called subclass or child class.
A class you cannot instantiate with `new`. It may contain abstract members that derived types must implement.
entries.example: `abstract class AuthHandler` — you create `LtiHandler`, not `AuthHandler` directly.

entries.plainDefinition: A class that cannot be inherited from. Use it to close a hierarchy.
entries.example: `sealed class LtiHandler : AuthHandler` — no further subclasses allowed.

blocks.text: Inheritance shares algorithm steps across a family of types. An auth provider family might share token validation and clock-skew checks in a base class, while `LtiHandler` and `OidcHandler` differ only in how they parse the raw token. Because C# enforces a single base class, you must choose that slot carefully — infrastructure dependencies belong in composition (previous topic), not in a deep base hierarchy.

blocks.title: Constructors are not inherited
blocks.body: Every derived class must call a base constructor — either implicitly (parameterless base) or explicitly with `base(...)`. If you forget, the compiler errors. Finalizers are also not inherited; you should avoid writing them (see module 14).

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Derived field initializers run
items.body: Field initializers in the derived type execute first in the initialization sequence.

items.title: Base constructor body runs
items.body: The base constructor initializes the base portion of the object. Use `base(args)` in the derived constructor's initializer list to pick which base constructor.

items.title: Derived constructor body runs
items.body: After the base is fully constructed, the derived constructor body executes. At this point all base fields are valid.

items.title: Object is ready
items.body: The fully initialized object can now be used. Avoid calling virtual methods from the base constructor — the derived override may run before derived fields are set.

diagram.title: Single inheritance and constructor chain
diagram.source:
flowchart TD

  AH --> LH[sealed LtiHandler]
  AH --> OH[sealed OidcHandler]
  NEW[new LtiHandler] -->|1 base ctor| AH
  NEW -->|2 derived ctor| LH
  NOTE[Only ONE class parent allowed]

snippet.label: Single base and constructor chaining
snippet.explanation: Line 1: abstract base with primary constructor capturing `issuer`. Line 6: derived type forwards `issuer` to the base via `: AuthHandler(issuer)`. Line 7: `ClientId` is a derived-only property. Line 9: `Parse` is the abstract method implementation. There is no second class parent — inject a logger instead.

snippet.label: abstract and sealed on the type
snippet.explanation: Line 2: `abstract` blocks `new Shape()`. Line 8: `sealed` blocks further inheritance. This is the production pattern: an open base (`Shape`) with a closed set of sealed derived types (`Circle`).

snippet.label: Base plus interfaces
snippet.explanation: Line 6: one base class (`Entity`) plus one interface (`IAuditable`). Line 12: `Order` inherits from `Entity` and automatically implements `IAuditable` through the base. You can list multiple interfaces but only one class.

blocks.title: Inheritance across languages
rows: extends one class; prototypes can be mutated at runtime
Prototype chain can change at runtime

blocks.title: Calling virtual methods from a base constructor
blocks.body: If the base constructor calls a virtual method, the derived override runs before derived field initializers complete. The override may see uninitialized derived state. Keep base constructors simple.

blocks.title: Public unsealed classes with no planned derived types
blocks.body: If you do not intend anyone to subclass your worker or DTO, mark it `sealed`. An unsealed public class is an open invitation for external inheritance you did not design for.

interviewTakeaways: One base class; constructors chain with base(...).
Constructors and finalizers are not inherited.
sealed is a design statement, not pessimism.
commonPitfalls: Forgetting that the base constructor runs before the derived body when reading instance virtual methods from a base ctor.
Public unsealed classes with no planned derived types.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JavaScript also requires super() before this in derived constructors. JavaScript can mutate the prototype at runtime; C# hierarchies are fixed in metadata.
TypeScript class extends one class and implements interfaces, similar on the surface. TypeScript implements is erased; C# implements is runtime-checkable.
